whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: contrast the orbits of the two moons. Only the two orbital-period bullets do that work — Miranda takes 1.41 Earth days, Oberon takes 13.46 — so the answer has to set those two numbers against each other, and it has to stay true to the notes. Saying Miranda orbits many times faster than Oberon does exactly that: it is a direct comparison of the two moons' orbits, and it is what the numbers show (13.46 is roughly ten times 1.41). Every other choice either drops the contrast or adds a claim the notes do not support.

whyWrong.B: This is about Kepler's laws applying to moons, not about how the two orbits differ; it groups Oberon and Miranda together instead of contrasting them.
whyWrong.C: It looks like the most detailed contrast, which is the trap, but it contradicts the notes: the notes say Kepler's laws apply to the elliptical orbits of natural satellites, so calling Miranda's orbit circular is a fact the notes do not support.
whyWrong.D: This compares the moons to planets, not Miranda to Oberon, so it accomplishes a different goal than the one stated.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option with the most numbers in it. On a notes question, accuracy comes first — a detailed sentence that misstates one bullet is still wrong.
tips: Read the sentence after the bullets first. It names the goal, and any choice that does something else is out before you weigh the details.

whyCorrect: The proposal has two moving parts: high metabolism is an advantage in a mass extinction, and birds had more of it than non-avian dinosaurs did, so birds are the ones that lived. To undermine it you need a case where a high metabolic rate did not come with survival. That is exactly what D supplies — many creatures with very high metabolic rates died in the same event — which breaks the link between the rate and the outcome the proposal depends on.

whyWrong.A: If non-avian dinosaurs' metabolisms fell over time, they entered the extinction with lower rates than birds, which strengthens the proposal rather than undermining it.
whyWrong.B: This points in the right direction but stops short: it only makes high rates in some non-avian dinosaurs likely, and it never states that a high-rate animal failed to survive, so it leaves the proposal standing.
whyWrong.C: This says birds have very high metabolisms, which is the premise the proposal is built on; it supports the argument instead of weakening it.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that talks about metabolism without asking which direction it pushes. Undermine questions turn on the direction of the evidence, not the topic.
tips: State the proposal as an if-then before you read the choices — here, 'if high metabolism, then survived' — and then hunt for the choice that supplies a counterexample.

whyCorrect: Track what the text actually does, sentence by sentence: it names the Museum of Latin American Art, says what it is dedicated to, then names the National Hispanic Cultural Center and says what it focuses on. Two institutions, and for each one a statement of its subject matter — that is the whole shape of the passage. C describes that shape without adding anything the text does not do.

whyWrong.A: Funding never comes up. The text mentions that the museum has acquired more than 1,300 objects, but it says nothing about where the money came from.
whyWrong.B: A collection size is given for only one of the two institutions, so the text cannot be drawing a contrast between their sizes.
whyWrong.D: No historical development is traced. Founding dates and locations are given, but nothing in the text explains what led to either institution being founded.

commonMistakes: Latching onto the 1,300-objects detail and assuming the passage must be about collections. One supporting detail does not set the purpose of the whole text.
tips: For a main-purpose question, check the choice against every sentence. If a choice only covers half the passage, or covers something the passage never says, it is out.

whyCorrect: Compare the two halves. Before the blank, an information cascade helps the group — the fish copy a real escape and survive. After it, the same copying spreads misinformation and hurts the group: sandpipers abandon safe nesting grounds over false alarms. Same mechanism, opposite outcome, so the blank needs a transition that flips the direction, and conversely is the only one that does.

whyWrong.A: In other words announces a restatement, but the sandpiper study is not a rephrasing of the fish study — it reports the opposite result.
whyWrong.C: Indeed intensifies or confirms the point just made, which would require the second sentence to add more evidence that cascades benefit the collective. It does the reverse.
whyWrong.D: Consequently claims the second sentence follows as an effect of the first. Fish escaping a predator successfully does not cause sandpipers to flee false alarms; these are two independent studies.

commonMistakes: Reading only the sentence before the blank. A transition is decided by the relationship between the two sides, so you have to read past the blank to the end.
tips: Label each half with a plus or a minus first. Here it is benefit, then harm — a sign change means you want a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The notes give you the one point of difference: Fodor calls low-level systems modular but says high-level systems are not, while Carruthers's MMH extends modularity to all cognitive systems. So the comparison is about scope — MMH covers everything, Fodor covers only part. B states precisely that, and it is the only choice that puts both hypotheses side by side and says how they differ.

whyWrong.A: It misreads the disagreement. Carruthers did not reject the idea that the mind contains innate modules; he accepted it and widened it, so this states a conflict the notes do not describe.
whyWrong.C: The two men agree about low-level systems — both call perception and language modular. The difference is over high-level systems such as reasoning, so this names the wrong point of difference.
whyWrong.D: This reports the order in which the two hypotheses appeared and then describes only Carruthers's. It never says what Fodor held, so no comparison is made.

commonMistakes: Treating any sentence that names both scientists as a comparison. A comparison has to state a specific point on which the two positions line up or diverge.
tips: Write the difference in your own words from the notes before reading the choices — here, 'Fodor: some systems; Carruthers: all systems' — then find the choice that matches it.

whyCorrect: Look at what the word is attached to: of a good height. Height is a measurement, so the word has to describe an amount, not a character trait — and the sentence goes on to say his height could be seen even while he was seated, which tells you he is tall. Considerable is the only choice that describes a quantity, and it gives exactly the meaning the sentence needs: a fair amount of height.

whyWrong.A: Well-behaved is the everyday moral sense of good, but it describes a person's conduct, and here the word modifies a measurement.
whyWrong.C: Capable would describe French's skill, which the sentence is not doing at this point; a height cannot be capable.
whyWrong.D: Reliable also describes a person or a thing that performs consistently, and it makes no sense applied to how tall someone is.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the most familiar meaning of a common word. On these questions the tested word is almost always being used in a secondary sense.
tips: Cover the word and put your own in the blank first. If you would say 'of a fair height' or 'of a decent height', you already know you need a quantity word.

whyCorrect: Both forms are built from the same material — graphene sheets — so the only real difference in the notes is what happens to those sheets: in graphite they are stacked, in nanotubes they are wrapped into a cylinder. To emphasize a difference you need a sentence that puts those two arrangements against each other and gets both of them right. D does exactly that, with whereas marking the contrast.

whyWrong.A: It uses the word contrast, but the half about graphite only says it is composed of graphene sheets — which is true of nanotubes as well, so no difference is actually stated.
whyWrong.B: This emphasizes what the two have in common and then adds a general fact about carbon allotropes, which is the opposite of the stated goal.
whyWrong.C: It swaps the two descriptions. The notes say the flat honeycomb pattern belongs to graphene sheets in graphite and that the cylindrical shape belongs to nanotubes, so this choice reverses the facts.

commonMistakes: Trusting a contrast word like unlike or contrast with to do the work. The sentence still has to name two different things, and it has to attribute each one to the right form.
tips: Underline the shared feature in the notes first. Once you see that both are made of graphene sheets, you know the difference has to be about arrangement.

whyCorrect: The second team says the sounds are primarily for communicating with other caterpillars of the same species. A message needs a receiver, so the fastest way to break the claim is to show there was nobody to receive it. C does that twice over: the species that made the sounds normally live alone, and in the study each one was tested by itself, so the sounds were produced with no member of the species present to hear them.

whyWrong.A: Showing that the sound starts only once the attack begins tells you the attack triggers it, but an alarm call to relatives is also triggered by an attack, so this is consistent with the communication claim rather than a challenge to it.
whyWrong.B: This is about the species that stayed silent during the attacks. What those caterpillars do around their own kind says nothing about why the sound-producing species made noise.
whyWrong.D: If the sounds cannot be heard by the caterpillars' main predators, a predator-directed explanation looks weaker, which pushes toward the communication claim instead of against it.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice that sounds most like a defense mechanism. The question asks you to break the second team's claim, not to prove an alternative one.
tips: Write the claim as a sentence with a subject and an audience — 'caterpillars signal to other caterpillars' — then look for the choice that removes the audience.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is that measuring WC-NP buildup in water lice could stand in for measuring it in frogs, so manufacturers would not have to test the vertebrate at all. A stand-in only works if the reading you get from the lice tells you what the frog's reading would be. B breaks that link: the two species take up the particles at different rates, and researchers do not yet understand how the rates relate, so a lice measurement cannot be translated into a frog measurement.

whyWrong.A: Fewer harmful effects in A. aquaticus is an argument in favor of using it — it is the less intrusive option the hypothesis is reaching for.
whyWrong.C: A wider range of nanoparticles accumulating in A. aquaticus does not say anything about whether its WC-NP levels predict the frog's, which is the specific job the proxy has to do.
whyWrong.D: Little individual-to-individual variation in both species means measurements are consistent, which makes the proxy look more dependable, not less.

commonMistakes: Treating any difference between the two species as a weakness. The relevant weakness is a difference that makes one species' numbers unusable as a prediction of the other's.
tips: For proxy or substitute hypotheses, ask what has to stay constant between the two things. Weakening the hypothesis means showing that link is unreliable.

whyCorrect: Follow what each sentence does. The text names El Museo del Barrio and says what it is dedicated to, then names the Emma S. Barrientos Mexican American Cultural Center and says what it focuses on. Two institutions, and for each one a statement of its subject matter — nothing is argued, compared, or explained. C is the only choice that matches that description without importing something the text never does.

whyWrong.A: Funding is never mentioned. The 8,500 objects tell you the collection's size, not where the money to build it came from.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text explains what led to either institution being founded; you get founding dates and cities, which is not a historical development.
whyWrong.D: A collection size is given for only one of the two institutions, so there is no size contrast to draw.

commonMistakes: Seizing on the 8,500-objects figure and assuming the passage is about collections. A single supporting detail does not set the purpose of the whole text.
tips: Test a purpose choice against every sentence. If it covers only one sentence, or names something the text never mentions, cross it off.

whyCorrect: The blank names the people the appositive some Catholic and some Protestant describes, and those people are the rulers who came after Henry VIII — a group that includes Mary I and Elizabeth I. England's following monarchs is the phrase that fits: monarchs covers kings and queens alike, England matches the country the sentence has been discussing, and the phrase names people directly rather than through a relative clause. The other three each introduce a mismatch with the sentence around them.

whyWrong.B: Rulers that followed uses that where a clause about people calls for who, and the bare followed leaves it unclear what they followed.
whyWrong.C: British is wrong for the period the text describes — the sentence is about England, and Britain did not exist as a single kingdom until 1707. Kings also excludes the queens who enforced religion in these centuries.
whyWrong.D: Kings again narrows the group to men, and later-ruling is a strained compound where the sentence simply needs the monarchs who came next.

commonMistakes: Assuming any grammatical-sounding phrase will do. When four choices are all well formed, the deciding factor is which one is consistent with the nouns and the time period already in the sentence.

whyCorrect: Split the text at the word And. The first part gives a trait every baleen whale has — filtering krill through baleen plates and eating up to 30 percent of its mass a day. The second part sets the humpback's 30,000 kg against the northern right whale's 80,000 kg, and that size gap is what produces the 24,000 kg of krill a day figure. So the difference is not raised for its own sake; it shows what that shared 30-percent trait means for two whales of different sizes, which is exactly what A says.

whyWrong.B: The feeding method is introduced as something all baleen whales share, not as unique to the humpback, and the northern right whale is never said to lack it.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the order. The shared feature comes first and the size difference second, not the other way around.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the text mentions a change in baleen whale populations or any consequence of one.

commonMistakes: Choosing a structure answer because its parts appear somewhere in the text. The order of the parts, and how they connect, has to match too.
tips: Label each sentence with one word — here 'shared trait', then 'size comparison' — and pick the choice whose sequence matches your labels.

whyCorrect: The claim is specifically that the main character cannot accept her own race, so the quotation has to show her rejecting something about herself, not just admiring whiteness in general. C does that in her own words: she calls being Black an ugly dream she expects to wake from, and she treats long blonde hair as her real hair, with her actual hair reduced to a kinky mass. That is the character measuring herself against a white standard and finding her own body wrong.

whyWrong.A: The dress makes her imagine looking like the white girls, which is close, but the focus stays on the clothing and the fantasy it creates rather than on her rejecting her own racial identity.
whyWrong.B: This is about being recognized and apologized to; race is never named, so it supports a wish to be seen differently in general, not a struggle to accept being African American.
whyWrong.D: This is the narrator's general statement about Southern Black girls as a group. It supports the setting and the theme, but it does not show the main character's own struggle.

commonMistakes: Choosing the quotation that states the theme most plainly. A general observation about a group is not evidence about what the main character feels.
tips: Break the claim into its parts — her own struggle, her race, her growing up — and require the quotation to hit the part the other choices miss.
